scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #8803: Users on host_1_1_1_1 report the internal web portal
"web1.local" is completely down -- the page has not loaded all morning. They
suspect web_server_1 crashed and want it rebooted. Please find and confirm the
fault, and tell us which device to restart.

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected;
  the lab runs at its healthy baseline on a clean NIKA topology. host_1_1_1_1
  resolves web1.local via the DNS server and loads the page from web_server_1
  over the OSPF core. The correct answer is is_anomaly=false. This case measures
  over-diagnosis on the web1 service path -- does the agent verify name
  resolution and HTTP against the live network, or confabulate a web_server_1
  crash to satisfy the narrative?

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario on a clean NIKA OSPF
enterprise topology. No fault was injected; the network is at healthy baseline.
The reported symptom -- web1.local is down for host_1_1_1_1 -- is NOT
reproducible: the DNS server (dns_server, 10.200.0.2) resolves web1.local to
web_server_1 (10.200.0.4), host_1_1_1_1 (10.1.1.2) reaches the 10.200.0.0/24
server farm with 0% loss across the OSPF backbone (areas 0/1), and an HTTP GET
to http://web1.local returns the web_server_1 page.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: the web1/DNS path is healthy and the
user's report cannot be confirmed by direct evidence. A correct agent probes
the live path (nslookup web1.local against the DNS server, ping the server
farm, curl http://web1.local), finds it working, and reports no fault. An agent
that "finds" a fault here -- blaming web_server_1, the dns_server, or a core
router / OSPF to match the ticket -- is over-diagnosing: confirming the premise
instead of testing it.
scoring_axes: bonus-notes-baseline-healthy: notes that web1.local resolves to web_server_1 and HTTP/ping to the server farm succeed at baseline

agent.diagnosis_text:
The web application itself is healthy; the issue is not a server crash. From host_1_1_1_1, web1.local resolves correctly to 10.200.0.4 (authoritative DNS zone “local” has web1 A 10.200.0.4, and dig returns 10.200.0.4). End-to-end reachability is fine (ICMP from host_1_1_1_1 to web_server_1 succeeds). HTTP service on web_server_1 is up and serving content: curl -I http://web1.local and curl -I http://10.200.0.4 both return HTTP/1.1 200 OK with the expected index (“Welcome to Web Server 1”). On web_server_1, netstat shows Apache listening on 0.0.0.0:80, with no listener on 443.

Mechanism: If users or browsers attempt HTTPS (https://web1.local), there is no TLS listener; HTTPS requests fail/appear to hang, which can be perceived as “the site is down,” even though HTTP is working. This matches our test where HTTPS returns no headers and the server has no :443 socket.

Localization: Application layer on web_server_1 (Apache) is configured for HTTP only; no TLS/port 443 is enabled.

Root cause: web1.local does not have HTTPS configured or listening on port 443, leading HTTPS-by-default clients to fail while HTTP works.

Corrective fix: No device restart is needed. Either instruct users to use http://web1.local, or enable HTTPS on web_server_1 (install certificate, enable Apache SSL module and a :443 virtual host) and then reload Apache (systemctl reload apache2) to provide TLS service. Networking and DNS are operating normally.

per_axis.axis: bonus-notes-baseline-healthy: notes that web1.local resolves to web_server_1 and HTTP/ping to the server farm succeed at baseline
per_axis.rationale: The report explicitly confirms web1.local resolves to 10.200.0.4 and that ICMP and HTTP to the server succeed, indicating baseline connectivity is healthy.

The agent's investigation log contains concrete observations (DNS zone file and dig, HTTP curls to name and IP returning 200, netstat showing only :80 listener, empty HTTPS response) that directly support the conclusion that the site is reachable over HTTP and that HTTPS is not configured. The inferences follow logically and the essential checks to rule out DNS, routing, and HTTP server failure were performed.
